title: What training does federal law require for foster parents and child welfare staff?
seoTitle: Title IV-E child welfare training rules
description: Title IV-E and Family First training rules: 75 percent federal match under 45 CFR 1356.60, foster parent preparation, caseworker and prevention plan duties.
shortAnswer: Federal child welfare law shapes training mainly through Title IV-E of the Social Security Act. States must certify that prospective foster parents are adequately prepared before placement, including in the reasonable and prudent parent standard, and must keep a combined Title IV-B and IV-E staff training plan. Under 45 CFR 1356.60(b), training costs qualify for 75 percent federal matching. The Family First Prevention Services Act added caseworker training and workforce duties for states running prevention programs.
keyTakeaways: 45 CFR 1356.60(b) makes training of title IV-E agency staff, and short-term training of current or prospective foster and adoptive parents and child care institution staff, eligible for 75 percent federal financial participation.
All training funded under Title IV-E must be included in the agency's Title IV-B training plan, which 45 CFR 1357.15(t) requires to be an ongoing staff development and training plan.
42 U.S.C. 671(a)(24) requires a certification that prospective foster parents will be prepared adequately before placement, with preparation continued after placement as necessary.
Child care institutions must have at least one on-site official trained to apply the reasonable and prudent parent standard in the same manner as foster parents.
States electing the Family First prevention program must describe how they will train and support caseworkers and build a workforce qualified in the evidence-based practices they select.
regulator: Children's Bureau, Administration for Children and Families (ACF), US Department of Health and Human Services
appliesTo: State and Tribal title IV-E agencies and the local agencies administering their plans
Current and prospective foster parents, adoptive parents and relative guardians
Staff of state-licensed or approved child care institutions and child welfare agencies serving title IV-E children
Court staff, agency attorneys, attorneys for children and parents, guardians ad litem and court-appointed special advocates (training eligible for match)

sections.heading: How does federal law regulate child welfare training?

blocks.text: Mostly through state plan conditions and funding, not through hour counts. Title IV-E of the Social Security Act, codified at [42 U.S.C. 670 and following](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/671), lists what a state plan must contain to receive federal foster care and adoption funding. Several plan items require preparation or training of specific groups, and [45 CFR 1356.60](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-B/chapter-XIII/subchapter-G/part-1356/section-1356.60) sets the federal share of training costs. Exact hours, curricula and delivery are set by each state or tribe.

This page summarizes the federal layer as at November 2026, from eCFR text current to November 5, 2026 and the current United States Code. It does not cover any single state's foster parent licensing hours, which vary widely.

sections.heading: What training costs can a title IV-E agency claim?

blocks.text: Training costs qualify for 75 percent federal financial participation, compared with 50 percent for most administrative costs. Under 45 CFR 1356.60(b)(1), the enhanced rate covers training personnel employed or preparing for employment by the title IV-E agency, and short-term training, including travel and per diem, for current or prospective foster or adoptive parents and members of state licensed or approved child care institutions caring for title IV-E children.

The statute is broader than the regulation's wording. [42 U.S.C. 674(a)(3)(B)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/674) extends the 75 percent rate to short-term training of relative guardians, staff of state-licensed or approved child welfare agencies, members of the staff of abuse and neglect courts, agency attorneys, attorneys representing children or parents, guardians ad litem and court-appointed special advocates, where the training increases their ability to support foster and adopted children.

items: 45 CFR 1356.60(b)(2): all training activities and costs funded under title IV-E must be included in the agency's title IV-B training plan.
45 CFR 1356.60(b)(3): short and long term training at educational institutions and in-service training may be provided under 45 CFR 235.63 to 235.66(a).
45 CFR 1356.60(c): other administrative costs, such as case management, recruitment and licensing of foster homes, are matched at 50 percent.

sections.heading: What must a state's child welfare training plan contain?

blocks.text: A staff development and training plan supporting the goals of the state's Child and Family Services Plan (CFSP). Under [45 CFR 1357.15(t)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-B/chapter-XIII/subchapter-G/part-1357/section-1357.15), the plan must address both title IV-B programs, must be combined with the title IV-E training plan, and training must be an ongoing activity drawing content from various disciplines and knowledge bases relevant to child and family services.

For an agency, this means one integrated plan rather than separate program silos, and a link between each training activity and a CFSP goal. The same discipline underpins [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations).

sections.heading: What preparation must foster parents receive?

blocks.text: Adequate preparation before a child is placed, continued after placement as needed. The state plan must include the certification in 42 U.S.C. 671(a)(24):

blocks.title: 42 U.S.C. 671(a)(24)
blocks.text: The state plan "includes a certification that, before a child in foster care under the responsibility of the State is placed with prospective foster parents, the prospective foster parents will be prepared adequately with the appropriate knowledge and skills to provide for the needs of the child, that the preparation will be continued, as necessary, after the placement of the child," and that the preparation shall include knowledge and skills relating to the reasonable and prudent parent standard.

The reasonable and prudent parent content must cover the developmental stages of a child's cognitive, emotional, physical and behavioral capacities, and applying the standard to decisions such as sports, field trips, overnight activities lasting one or more days, signing permission slips and arranging transportation.

Under 42 U.S.C. 671(a)(10)(B), each contract with a child care institution must require at least one official on site who is designated to apply the reasonable and prudent parent standard and who is trained in the same manner as prospective foster parents.

sections.heading: Which federal provisions require caseworker training?

blocks.text: Three plan provisions name caseworker training directly.

items: Sex trafficking, 42 U.S.C. 671(a)(9)(C): the state agency must have policies and procedures, including relevant training for caseworkers, for identifying, documenting and determining services for children and youth who are, or are at risk of being, sex trafficking victims.

Relative foster homes, 42 U.S.C. 671(a)(36)(C): a state that waives nonsafety licensing standards for relative foster family homes must report how caseworkers are trained to use the waiver authority, and (D) the steps it is taking to improve caseworker training.

Prevention services, 42 U.S.C. 671(e)(5)(B)(viii): a state electing the title IV-E prevention program must describe how it will train and support caseworkers in assessing what children and families need, connecting with families, accessing and delivering trauma-informed and evidence-based services, and overseeing the continuing appropriateness of services.

blocks.text: For agencies handling trafficking risk across health and social care, the [human trafficking training page](/regulations/human-trafficking-training-requirements-healthcare) covers related state mandates.

sections.heading: What workforce duties did the Family First Prevention Services Act add?

blocks.text: The [Family First Prevention Services Act](https://acf.gov/cb/programs-services/title-iv-e-prevention-program), enacted as part of Public Law 115-123, created optional title IV-E funding for time-limited prevention services: mental health, substance abuse and in-home parent skill-based programs for children who are candidates for foster care, pregnant or parenting foster youth, and their parents or kin caregivers. A state that elects it must include a prevention plan component in its title IV-E plan.

Under 42 U.S.C. 671(e)(5)(B)(vii), that component must describe the steps the state is taking to support and enhance a competent, skilled and professional child welfare workforce to deliver trauma-informed and evidence-based services, including ensuring staff are qualified to provide the promising, supported or well-supported practice models selected, and developing prevention plans and risk assessments. Services must be trauma-informed, which 671(e)(4)(B) defines as provided under an organizational structure and treatment framework that involves understanding, recognizing and responding to the effects of all types of trauma.

Family First also defined qualified residential treatment programs in [42 U.S.C. 672(k)(4)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/672). These must have a trauma-informed treatment model and registered or licensed nursing and other licensed clinical staff available 24 hours a day and 7 days a week, and must be accredited by an approved independent body. The statute does not set training hours for QRTP staff, but the trauma-informed model sets the content their training must support.

sections.heading: How can an agency map federal duties to training evidence?

blocks.text: Federal reviewers and auditors look at two things: whether a training cost was properly claimed and whether a plan certification is backed by practice. The table below is an illustrative register.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each training activity to the plan provision it supports and to the funding category it is claimed under, so the same record answers a program review question and a cost allocation question. Evidence-based practice models chosen for prevention can be mapped to the staff competencies they require. See [government and public sector](/industries/government-defence).

faqs.q: How many hours of training must foster parents complete under federal law?
faqs.a: Federal law does not set an hour count. 42 U.S.C. 671(a)(24) requires a state plan certification that prospective foster parents will be prepared adequately before placement, including in the reasonable and prudent parent standard. Hours and curricula are set by each state's foster home licensing rules.

faqs.q: What is the federal match rate for child welfare training?
faqs.a: Under 45 CFR 1356.60(b) and 42 U.S.C. 674(a)(3), eligible title IV-E training is matched at 75 percent federal financial participation. Most other administrative costs of the title IV-E plan, under 1356.60(c), are matched at 50 percent.

faqs.q: Can training for court staff and attorneys be claimed under Title IV-E?
faqs.a: The statute allows it. 42 U.S.C. 674(a)(3)(B) includes short-term training of abuse and neglect court staff, agency attorneys, attorneys representing children or parents, guardians ad litem and court-appointed special advocates at 75 percent, where it improves support for foster and adopted children. Claims must follow the agency's training plan and cost allocation.

faqs.q: Does Family First require specific caseworker training hours?
faqs.a: No. States electing the title IV-E prevention program must describe in their prevention plan how they will train and support caseworkers and ensure staff are qualified in the selected practice models, under 42 U.S.C. 671(e)(5)(B)(vii) and (viii). The content and hours are for the state to define.
